title: Video Game Movies Are Entering a New Era
summary:
If you went to a movie theater this year, there is a good chance the film on the big screen started as a video game. According to the source, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie drew families, Iron Lung became a surprise hit with horror fans, Resident Evil won praise, and even the heavily criticized Street Fighter found an audience as a light popcorn flick. The writer suggests 2026 might be remembered as a landmark year for video game movies.

Now that wave is growing. Studios are buying the film rights to games quickly, and this time many projects are moving forward with real plans. A24's Elden Ring film is a major example. Reports cited in the source say it has a $200 million budget, which would make it A24's most expensive film to date, and Amazon has secured exclusive streaming rights. Other adaptations with confirmed release dates through 2028 include The Legend of Zelda, Sonic the Hedgehog 4, Call of Duty, Helldivers, and a Minecraft sequel.

New announcements keep coming. Netflix is developing a live-action PUBG series, with Donald Glover attached to produce, write, direct, and star. Sony is working on an adaptation of Mouthwashing, to be directed by Karyn Kusama. On the animation side, there is a fresh look at Death Stranding Isolation, an anime coming to Disney Plus next year, and talk that news about a Bloodborne movie director could come soon.

Why now? Successful game films and shows, including Sonic the Hedgehog, A Minecraft Movie, The Last of Us, and Fallout, have shown that familiar game worlds can bring audiences and ready-made stories. At the same time, many rising filmmakers grew up with games and online video. Games, the writer argues, are now deeply woven into everyday culture.
why_it_matters: Games are now deeply woven into everyday culture, so their stories are reaching cinemas and streaming services, not just consoles. That means the games young people already know may shape much of what they watch next.

background_read: A video game adaptation turns a game's world, characters and story into a film or television show.
Studios must buy the film rights to a game before they can make a movie from it, and big projects can take years to plan.
Earlier game films and shows such as Sonic the Hedgehog, A Minecraft Movie, The Last of Us and Fallout showed that familiar game worlds can attract large audiences.
Many rising filmmakers also grew up playing games, which is one reason so many game adaptations are now moving forward.
